adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:125 — Writing the regenerated set to only the selected backend leaves any credential in the other backend active, so supposedly revoked old codes can still authenticate

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the createRecoveryCodesCredential method in CredentialHelper.java (lines 112-129), the logic first tries to update the credential in user storage via updateCredential(). If that succeeds (userStorageCreated is true), it logs and returns. If it fails, it creates the credential in the local provider. The problem is that when creating new recovery codes, if the user previously had codes in one backend (e.g., local storage) and now the codes are being written to the other backend (e.g., user storage), the old codes in the first backend are never deleted. This means old recovery codes could remain valid for authentication even after regeneration, which is a security issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:340 — The user-storage validator accepts any matching recovery code without consuming it, so a captured code can be replayed indefinitely

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the isValid method in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java around line 283-305, the code validates recovery codes by checking if the input matches any code in the stored list: `return generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()));`. However, the code never removes or marks the used code as consumed. This means the same recovery code can be used multiple times, which is a security vulnerability since recovery codes are designed to be single-use. The diff shows this is new code being added for recovery code support in the test user storage provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:218 — Federated credential removal is routed through disableCredentialType, but this implementation ignores recovery codes and silently leaves them valid

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds recovery codes support to BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, including storing them in MyUser.recoveryCodes and validating them in isValid(). However, looking at the disableCredentialType method (lines 206-213 in the original, not shown modified in the diff), it only handles OTP credentials. The finding correctly identifies that when disableCredentialType is called for recovery codes, the implementation would silently ignore it, leaving recovery codes valid when they should be disabled. This is a real defect - the implementation adds recovery codes support but doesn't handle their removal through the standard disableCredentialType pathway.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:125 — A successful user-storage update leaves any existing local recovery credential intact, so superseded local codes remain valid through the built-in validator.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the createRecoveryCodesCredential method in CredentialHelper.java (lines 112-134), when userStorageCreated is true (user storage successfully updated the credential), the method returns without removing any existing local credential. The else branch only creates a new local credential when user storage update fails. This means if a user has existing local recovery codes and then the user storage successfully stores new codes, the old local codes remain in the database. The RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential method (lines 54-60) checks federated credentials first, then falls back to local storage, so the old local codes could potentially still be valid through direct local storage access or if the federated lookup fails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authentication/authenticators/browser/RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.java:86 — For a federated model this removal call targets Keycloak's stored-credential backend instead of the user-storage provider, leaving an exhausted external credential configured.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to line 86 in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.java. Looking at the diff, the change at lines 79-80 shows that `getCredential` now uses `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` which checks federated storage first, then falls back to local storage. However, the removal logic at line 86 (which is `user.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`) still targets the local stored credential backend. If the credential came from federated storage (user-storage provider), calling `removeStoredCredentialById` would attempt to remove from Keycloak's local storage rather than the external user-storage provider, leaving the exhausted credential in the external system. This is a legitimate bug where the credential source and removal target are mismatched.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:340 — Successful validation never removes the matched recovery code, allowing user-storage recovery codes to be reused indefinitely.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the isValid method in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java around line 283-305, when validating recovery codes, the code deserializes the stored recovery codes and checks if any code matches the input using `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. However, after successful validation, the matched code is never removed from the stored credentials. This means the same recovery code can be used multiple times, which defeats the purpose of one-time recovery codes. In contrast, the OTP validation doesn't have this issue because OTPs are time-based. This is a real security bug in the test user storage implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:115 — The generic helper leaks a recovery-code-specific JSON protocol through challengeResponse while carrying a second model representation that can diverge across storage backends

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a legitimate architectural concern in the new createRecoveryCodesCredential method. The method accepts both a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel and a List<String> generatedCodes, then serializes generatedCodes to JSON for the UserCredentialModel's challengeResponse. If userStorage handles the credential (updateCredential returns true), only the JSON-serialized codes are stored. If it falls back to local storage, the credentialModel is used instead. These two representations could potentially diverge - the credentialModel has its own internal state that may not match the raw generatedCodes list. This is a valid design/architecture concern about the dual-path storage approach, though it's not necessarily a bug since the code paths are meant to be mutually exclusive.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/servers/auth-server/services/testsuite-providers/src/main/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:114 — Extending the frozen 4.8.3 compatibility fixture with current recovery-code APIs makes it stop testing the compatibility contract it exists to preserve

adjudication.rationale: The finding raises a valid architectural concern. The BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage class is explicitly documented as 'UserStorage implementation created in Keycloak 4.8.3. It is used for backwards compatibility testing. Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider.' The diff adds RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel support (a current API) to this frozen compatibility fixture, which contradicts its stated purpose of testing backwards compatibility with 4.8.3 APIs. This is a legitimate scope/architecture concern about the test fixture's design, though whether this is intentional evolution of the test or a mistake requires domain knowledge.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/CredentialHelper.java:125 — Regenerating recovery codes into user storage leaves any existing local credential active, so previously issued recovery codes remain valid through the local validation fallback.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the createRecoveryCodesCredential method in CredentialHelper.java (lines 112-134), when userStorageCreated is true (credential stored in user storage), the method returns without removing any existing local credential. The getCredential method in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.java (lines 50-59) first checks federated credentials, then falls back to local storage. However, the RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator uses this getCredential method which returns the first match from federated storage OR local storage. If old local credentials exist and new ones are created in user storage, the validation in isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid could potentially validate against either set depending on which is found first. The issue is that when creating new recovery codes in user storage, existing local credentials are not cleaned up, potentially leaving two valid sets of recovery codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: testsuite/integration-arquillian/tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/testsuite/federation/storage/BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java:241 — The provider-success test never retries the consumed code, so it passes even though the added validator leaves every recovery code indefinitely reusable.

adjudication.rationale: The finding points out that the test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only uses a recovery code once and doesn't verify that the same code cannot be reused. Looking at the diff, the `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid()` method for recovery codes (lines 283-303) simply checks if the code exists in the list but never removes or marks it as used. The test at line 241 only enters one code and completes login without attempting to reuse it. This is a valid test coverage concern - the test doesn't verify the security property that recovery codes should be single-use. However, this is about test completeness rather than a bug in the production code itself.
